# How to Use Alexa+ for Hands-Free Cooking

> **In short:** Alexa+ can read recipes aloud, set timers, and convert measurements by voice. You need an Echo, the free Alexa app, and an Amazon account. There's no dedicated recipe feature — it just reads text aloud, and exact phrasing can be hit-or-miss.

Your hands are sticky with cookie dough and the next instruction says "fold in the chocolate chips." Fumbling for the phone means wiping flour across the screen and losing your spot. Alexa+ is Amazon's upgraded voice assistant — you speak naturally, it reads the next step out loud, and your phone stays dry on the counter. This guide walks you through cooking one recipe without ever touching your screen. (Exact behavior varies by Echo model and Alexa+ version; the steps below include fallbacks for when your device does something different.)

## Before you start

- **An Amazon account** (free). If you don't have one, sign up on Amazon's website in about three minutes.
- **An Alexa-enabled device** — any Echo speaker (Echo, Echo Dot, Echo Show, or a third-party speaker with Alexa built in). Without one, this guide is not for today.
- **The free Alexa app** on your phone, signed in to the same Amazon account, already paired with your Echo. New to setup? Plug in the Echo, open the app, and follow the "Add device" prompts — about five minutes.
- **A recipe in plain text** — copied from a webpage into a note, or typed in your own words.
- **Total time:** about 15 minutes the first time. After that, under a minute per recipe.

## Step 1 — Confirm Alexa+ is on your device

Open the **Alexa app** on your phone. At the bottom of the screen is a row of tabs — tap the one labeled **Devices** (usually second or third from the left, often with a small speaker icon). A list of your Alexa devices appears. Tap the Echo you plan to cook with, then scroll the detail page that opens. Look for any label, banner, or badge mentioning **"Alexa+"**. According to Amazon, the upgraded experience is rolling out gradually, so it may appear near the top as a colored chip on some devices and not at all on others. If you see it, the conversational features in later steps are more likely to work as described. If your device page looks plain, you may still have the older Alexa experience and behavior may differ.

💬 Example: ask yourself, "Do I see anything labeled Alexa+ on this device's page?"

You'll know it worked when you can clearly tell whether your device shows the Alexa+ label, so you know what to expect in the next steps.

## Step 2 — Put the recipe text on your phone

Alexa+ reads text aloud — that's general reading behavior, not a built-in recipe tool. The cleaner the text, the better it works. Open the recipe on your phone and either **copy the URL** to your clipboard or **copy the full ingredient list and steps** into a single note in your phone's Notes app. Skip screenshots, PDF scans, and photos of cookbook pages — Alexa+ generally cannot read those. Whether Alexa+ can fetch and read a recipe from a spoken URL is not confirmed; pasting the text yourself is the safer bet for now.

💬 Example: paste a recipe's full text into a note titled with the dish name, like "Chocolate chip cookies."

You'll know it worked when you have one clean block of recipe text ready in a note, and your phone is somewhere dry away from the work zone.

## Step 3 — Get within easy voice range of your Echo

Smart speakers hear best when you're **in the same room, about 3 to 6 feet (1 to 2 meters) away** — close enough for normal-volume talking, far enough that pot steam does not constantly hit the microphone. In a kitchen with an island, place the Echo on the counter edge nearest where you'll stand; against a back wall it may struggle over a loud exhaust fan. The microphones live at the top of the device, so face it when you speak. There is no exact right spot — closer is generally better than farther. Quick test before you start cooking so you are not surprised mid-recipe.

💬 Example: stand at your main prep spot, face the Echo, and say "Alexa" at normal speaking volume. If the light ring at the top glows blue, the Echo heard you.

You'll know it worked when the Echo's light ring lights up blue every time you say "Alexa" from where you usually cook.

## Step 4 — Try reading the recipe through Alexa+

Alexa+ has no dedicated recipe mode. What it usually does well is read text aloud — the exact wording that triggers that is not officially documented, so think of the phrases below as starting points to experiment with. Stand where you confirmed the Echo can hear you and try a request along these lines, slowly and clearly: **"Alexa, read me the recipe in my notes."** Then either read the text aloud yourself or open the note you prepared and let Alexa+ read it. Behavior varies by device and version — it may repeat the ingredients, ask if you're ready, or begin reading the first step. If the first attempt doesn't read smoothly, try a close variation such as **"Alexa, read this recipe step by step"** or **"Alexa, read my [dish name] recipe."** Pause a second after each request so the Echo has time to respond.

💬 Example: *"Alexa, read my cookie recipe step by step."* Then either read it out loud yourself or let Alexa+ read the note you prepared.

You'll know it worked when Alexa+ reads the recipe aloud in some form — whether all at once, broken into steps, or after a quick clarifying question. If it doesn't read at all, try a different phrasing, or revisit Step 1 to confirm Alexa+ is enabled on your device.

## Step 5 — Move through the recipe with simple voice commands

To control the flow, use plain language. **"Next"** usually moves to the following step, and **"repeat that"** usually re-reads the current one. **"Pause"** typically stops the reading; **"continue"** or **"resume"** picks it back up. If you lose track, try **"what step am I on?"** — Alexa+ may or may not answer, depending on your version. **"Go back one step"** often works for re-hearing cook times. These exact phrases aren't officially documented for recipe reading, so a little trial and error is normal — if one doesn't work, try a close synonym. From ingredients to plated dish, you should not need to touch your phone.

💬 Example: while kneading dough, say *"Alexa, next"* — no phone, no tapping, no flour on a screen.

You'll know it worked when you finish the recipe and realize your phone never left the counter, even after long pauses.

## Step 6 — Set cooking timers without breaking your flow

Hands covered in oil? Say **"Alexa, set a timer for 12 minutes"** without leaving the recipe. Timers run in the background and chime when time is up. Name them so you remember which is which: *"Alexa, set a pasta timer for 9 minutes"* and *"Alexa, set a sauce timer for 4 minutes."* To cancel one, say **"cancel the pasta timer"** by name. Honest limit: timers and recipe reading are separate, so a chiming timer may overlap with Alexa+ speaking. If that happens, say **"Alexa, stop"** to silence the timer, then **"repeat that"** to hear the step again. Named timers are an officially supported feature, so these phrases usually work as expected.

💬 Example: *"Alexa, set an oven timer for 12 minutes."* When it chimes, say *"Alexa, stop. Alexa, continue."*

You'll know it worked when the timer chimes on time and you can cancel each one by name, without ever opening the app.

## Step 7 — Convert measurements on the fly

Many online recipes use grams and milliliters. Pause the recipe and ask **"how much is 200 grams of flour in cups?"** — Alexa+ usually answers in US cups and ounces. You can ask the reverse too: *"how many tablespoons in a quarter cup?"* After the answer, say **"continue"** to return to the recipe. Honest limit: Alexa+ is a general assistant, not a baking-scale converter, so for delicate pastry you may still want to double-check the math on a phone later. Conversions are general-purpose and usually work, but for precision baking, treat them as a starting point, not gospel.

💬 Example: *"Alexa, how many cups is 200 grams of butter?"* then *"Alexa, continue."*

You'll know it worked when you hear a clear conversion in US measurements and the recipe picks up at the same step.

## Common mistakes

- **Assuming Alexa+ can see your phone screen.** It doesn't. If you want it to use a recipe on a webpage, paste the text into a note or read it aloud — copying silently to your clipboard won't transfer.
- **Speaking too fast or mumbling.** Read ingredients and steps slowly, in a steady voice, from your prepared text. If Alexa+ mishears, rephrase the whole request rather than repeating one word.
- **Expecting one magic phrase to work.** Voice command behavior for recipe reading is not officially documented. If "Alexa, read my recipe" doesn't trigger it, try "Alexa, read my [dish name] recipe" or "Alexa, read this recipe step by step." A little trial and error is normal.
- **Letting timers pile up.** Three timers chiming at once is worse than none. Cancel by name as you go: *"cancel the sauce timer."*

## What this means for you

- **In everyday life:** The recipe-on-the-counter, phone-on-the-couch setup becomes normal again. You'll cook more often because the friction of cleaning your hands between steps is gone — and you'll stop losing your place at step four of seven.
- **For your business or work:** If you teach cooking, host supper clubs, or run a food-related small business, you can rehearse recipes aloud, time multiple dishes in parallel without a stopwatch, and record recipe text for handouts — all from one Echo.
- **If you're just getting started:** The voice commands from Step 5 — *next, repeat, continue, what step am I on* — transfer to any numbered list you give Alexa+, not just recipes. Try the same hands-free flow with a workout, a bedtime checklist, or a DIY repair.

## Try it now

In the next two minutes: pick a recipe you know by heart, paste its text into a note, then say *"Alexa, read me this recipe step by step."* Just listen — don't cook yet. You'll feel in those two minutes why this is worth setting up before the next messy recipe.
